title: Elon Musk Clashes With Economist Editor, Says Public Hates Media More Than Him
excerpt: The Tesla CEO told The Economist's Zanny Minton Beddoes that journalists have a 15 percent favorability rating, dismissing her challenge over his influence on European politics.
body:
• Elon Musk told The Economist's editor-in-chief that "a lot more people hate you and the media more than you realize" during a testy interview at Tesla's Texas Gigafactory.
  • Zanny Minton Beddoes challenged Musk over his efforts to influence European politics, saying his wealth and X platform gave him outsized power abroad.
  • Musk cited his 250 million X followers as evidence of support and claimed the favorable view of journalists was around 15 percent.
  • A 2025 Gallup poll found that 28 percent of Americans had trust in news media to report fully and fairly — a record low.

Elon Musk fired back at The Economist's editor-in-chief Zanny Minton Beddoes during an interview at Tesla's Gigafactory in Texas on Thursday, dismissing her suggestion that people loathed him and turning the criticism back on the media industry.

"I think a lot more people hate you and the media more than you realize," Musk told Beddoes, after she confronted him over his efforts to influence European politics through his X platform.

The European Politics Question

Beddoes challenged Musk on his support for right-wing European political parties, arguing that his wealth, ownership of X, and his 250 million followers gave him unusual power to shape politics in countries where he does not live.

"Why should you be able to shape European politics? You don't even live there," Beddoes said. "It's why people loathe you. I mean, some people do loathe you."

Musk was unmoved. "Maybe some people do loathe me, and that's probably true. I don't care," he said. "But the fact that, as you pointed out, a quarter billion people follow me is that I think a lot more people actually like me than don't."

"The shoe is on the other foot. They hate you. They hate you far more than they hate me. I think you're the problem. The media."

— Elon Musk to The Economist's Zanny Minton Beddoes

The exchange followed a longer disagreement about Musk's political interventions in Europe. Musk urged Germans to vote for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party and interviewed its leader, Alice Weidel, on X ahead of Germany's 2025 federal election. Reuters reported he promoted the party in at least two dozen posts over two months. Beddoes described the parties Musk backed as far right; Musk rejected the label.

"I literally said, look, I believe in safe cities, secure borders and sensible spending with respect to government," Musk said. "That doesn't make me right wing at all in the least."

The Trust Deficit

Musk then pivoted to the media's own standing with the public. "Do you realize the media is despised?" he said. "The view of journalists — a favorable view of journalists is like 15 percent."

Beddoes acknowledged that trust in American journalism was low but argued that polarization on social media, including on X, contributed to the problem. "I think in part there have been mistakes by journalists and journalism. I totally acknowledge that," she said. "But I also think that the kind of polarized environment, particularly on social media, fostered by the kinds of things you are pushing on X, actually helps make this worse."

Public confidence in the press has indeed cratered. A 2025 Gallup poll found that 28 percent of Americans had a great deal or fair amount of trust in newspapers, television, and radio to report the news fully, accurately, and fairly — a record low for the survey.

Broader Implications

The clash underscores the growing tension between legacy media institutions and tech platforms over who shapes public discourse. For diaspora communities that increasingly rely on platforms like X for cross-border news and political information, the erosion of trust in both traditional media and social media platforms complicates the information landscape in every direction.
